name: Felix Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I run a dozer at the open-cut coal mine, mostly on the dumps, spreading what the trucks tip so the next lot has somewhere to go, and sometimes cutting pads for the drills. I've been on the same D10, a big track dozer, for six years, and I know every rattle in it. Shift starts at six, I'm usually there at a quarter past five with a thermos. It's not exciting, but I'm good at keeping a dump square.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being left alone to do a job properly. What wears me out is the back. Twelve hours of track vibration and my lower back is gone by Thursday. And money's always tight. Rosa works at the bakery counter in the supermarket, we've got Mateo, who's 11, and Lucia, who's 7, and the mortgage on our place on Station Road. I'm on the lower rate because I came in through a labour hire company and they never bumped me up properly when I went permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, to be honest. I'm not the type to post things. If someone at crib brought it up I'd say good, now can we talk about the footy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. The coal won't last forever anyway, the mine's got maybe fifteen years, so that's my worry, not computers. But if nothing changes, that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Turn up, do the shift, go home. Maybe get the back looked at properly, which I keep putting off because the physio's $90 a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. That's how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mine has about fifteen years. Do you think about that much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. When they announce something about coal in the news, Rosa asks me what I'll do. I tell her I'll be 58 by then and I'll worry about it at 55.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever used one of the AI apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Mateo tried to show me one, he asked it to write a poem about a dozer and it did. It was all right. I don't need a poem about a dozer, I need a dozer.

S0.say: He wouldn't post anything and would brush it off at crib, saying good, now let's talk about football. He isn't one to make statements.
S0.think: It means he keeps doing what he's doing. His real long-term worry is the coal running out in about fifteen years, not computers.
S0.do: Carries on with the same shifts and routine. Might finally get his back treated, which he keeps putting off because the physio costs $90 a visit.
S0.feel: Fine and normal, which is how he likes it.
S0.quote: I don't need a poem about a dozer, I need a dozer.
S0.fieldNote: He is a man of short answers who values routine above all. His long-range worry is the mine's coal running out, which he defers until he's 55. He has never used AI and sees no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. Every few years there's some big change coming and most of it doesn't come. I'd keep my head down and not get into arguments about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't like it. They're already running driverless trucks at a couple of the big coal mines, and if the trucks go, they'll want the dozers next. I'm not a computer person and I'm not going to become one. So I'd be hoping I'm one of the ones they keep for the jobs the machines can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually announces before doing anything. At home I'd stop the extras, like the takeaway and the fishing trips, and try to have a bit more in the bank. I'd make sure I'm the best dozer operator on that dump, so they'd want to keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my gut. Like when you hear a new noise in the machine and you don't know yet if it's anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make sure you're the best on the dump. Would that be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. A machine doesn't get a sore back. But it's the one thing I know how to do, so it's what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, at the kitchen table after the kids are in bed. Not the blokes at work, they'd just make jokes about robots. And maybe my brother-in-law, he's a fitter, he hears what the bosses are planning before we do.

S1.say: He'd say we'll see, since most predicted big changes never come. He'd keep his head down and avoid arguments.
S1.think: He doesn't like it: driverless trucks already exist and dozers could be next. He won't become a computer person, so he'd hope to be kept for jobs machines can't do yet.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company announces before acting. Cuts takeaway and fishing trips to build savings, and tries to be the best dozer operator on the dump so they keep him.
S1.feel: Uneasy in his gut, like hearing a new noise in the machine.
S1.quote: Probably not, if I'm honest. A machine doesn't get a sore back.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is calm but privately he sees dozers following trucks into automation. His only plan is to be good at his job, and he admits that may not be enough. With thin savings and a firm refusal to learn new tech, he's under real pressure even in the moderate picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not something I can do anything about. It's above my pay grade, it's governments and big companies. I'd just tell people to look after their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished. I'm 43, I can run a dozer, and that's what I've got. Rosa's job at the bakery would go too, probably. With less than a month of money in the bank, we wouldn't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those two years, I'd work every overtime shift and pay down whatever I could. Once it arrived, if I lost the job I'd probably have to sell the house before the bank took it, and we'd move in with Rosa's mother in her three-bedroom place. I'd take whatever government help there was, even though I've never asked for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being buried. I wouldn't sleep, and I wouldn't tell anyone that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for other work in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where? The only other jobs here are at the mine, the supermarket and the council. If robots are doing hands-on work, the council grader goes too. I'd look, but I don't know what I'd be looking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're going to live with Nana for a while, and that it's an adventure. Lucia would believe me. Mateo would know, he's like his mother, he reads the room.

S2.say: He'd say it's above his pay grade, a matter for governments and big companies. He'd just tell people to look after their families.
S2.think: He thinks he's finished: at 43 he can run a dozer and little else, and his partner's bakery job would likely go too. With under a month of savings they wouldn't last.
S2.do: Works every overtime shift in the two years before to pay down debt. If laid off, sells the house before the bank takes it, moves in with his mother-in-law and takes government help for the first time.
S2.feel: Like being buried; sleepless, and telling no one.
S2.quote: That we're going to live with Nana for a while, and that it's an adventure. Lucia would believe me.
S2.fieldNote: His public shrug hides a private sense that he's finished. He sees no other work in town and doesn't know what he'd even look for. Selling the house and moving in with family is the only plan he can name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, look after your own. Maybe I'd say the government should make sure the mortgage banks go easy on people. I'm not one for marches, but that seems fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be 48. That's still too young to stop and too old to start over, so the outcome's the same. The difference is I'd have time to get the house paid down a bit and maybe not lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by getting the mortgage down, putting any overtime and the tax refund straight on it. I'd hold on at the mine as long as they'd have me. In the last year or so, I'd look at whether there's anything driving-related left, but I wouldn't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. More like a bad forecast than a storm on top of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you won't retrain. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the company paid and it was something with machines, like servicing these robot dozers. My brother-in-law reckons they'll need fitters for a while. I'd think about it, but I'm not promising. I don't do well in classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car. We don't really need it, Rosa can walk to the supermarket. That's about $300 a month with the loan and insurance.

S3.say: He'd say look after your own, and maybe that government should make banks go easy on mortgage holders. He's not one for marches but thinks that's fair.
S3.think: At 48 he'd be too young to stop and too old to start over, so the end result is the same. The extra time just lets him pay down the house and maybe keep it.
S3.do: Puts overtime and tax refunds onto the mortgage and sells the second car to save about $300 a month. Holds on at the mine as long as possible and might consider servicing robot dozers if the company paid.
S3.feel: Worried, more like a bad forecast than a storm overhead.
S3.quote: More like a bad forecast than a storm on top of you.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him one clear goal: protect the house. He opened the door slightly to training if it was paid and hands-on, through his brother-in-law's hint about fitter work. He stays wary of anything in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. I wouldn't get worked up about it in public. People will worry about it when it's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is actually all right for me. The coal was going to run out around then anyway. I'd be 53, the mortgage would be smaller, and the kids would be close to grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep paying down the house. Maybe in year five or six I'd look at a fitter's course if the company was paying, because by then I'd know if that's a real job. Mostly I'd make sure Mateo and Lucia don't plan on the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy still, but I can live with it. It's the same feeling I've had about the coal for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Mateo and Lucia to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their heads, like a plumber or a nurse. I don't know what's safe. I'd just tell them don't put everything on one company like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years different from five for you, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Five years I'm still paying off the house when it hits. Ten years I might own most of it. That's the whole difference for me, the house.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, and wouldn't get worked up publicly. People will worry when it's close.
S4.think: Ten years is all right for him, since the coal was due to run out about then anyway. At 53 the mortgage would be smaller and the kids nearly grown.
S4.do: Keeps working and paying down the house, and may look at a company-paid fitter's course in year five or six. Steers his kids away from planning on the mine.
S4.feel: Uneasy but livable, like the long-standing feeling about the coal running out.
S4.quote: Ten years I might own most of it. That's the whole difference for me, the house.
S4.fieldNote: For him every version of the AGI pictures comes down to one question: will the house be paid off. Ten years lines up with the mine's expected closing, which strangely reassures him. His advice to his kids is not to rely on one company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the one where we lose the house. What would help is if the banks had to give you a year's break on the mortgage if your job goes to a machine, and some real work in the town, even if it's not mining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you got it. Maybe just that most of us don't hate technology, we just can't afford to be wrong. One bad year and you're done.

headlineQuote: Most of us don't hate technology, we just can't afford to be wrong. One bad year and you're done.
portrait: Felix Torres is a 43-year-old dozer operator at an open-cut coal mine who likes being left alone to do a job properly. He has a sore back, a partner who works at the supermarket bakery, two kids, a mortgage and almost no savings, and he has never used AI. In public he shrugs at every scenario, but privately he sees dozers following trucks into automation and admits being good at his job may not save it. Each AGI picture comes down for him to whether the house is paid off before the work goes.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it's the one where his family loses the house.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that banks give a year's mortgage break when a job goes to a machine, and some real work in town, even outside mining.
